title: Terrorist and Proliferation Financing Investigations
summary: An advanced eight-module programme equipping analysts, investigators and prosecutors to detect, investigate and disrupt terrorist and proliferation financing.
intro: This training programme equips FIU analysts, investigators and prosecutors to investigate terrorist and proliferation financing, from how funds are raised and moved to non-profit sector risks, targeted financial sanctions and intelligence sharing.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give specialist analysts, investigators and prosecutors an advanced understanding of how terrorist and proliferation networks raise, move and use funds, and of the tools available to detect and disrupt them. Participants leave able to develop financial intelligence on these threats, apply targeted financial sanctions, protect the non-profit sector proportionately and build cases with domestic and international partners.
sections.What It Covers: The terrorist and proliferation financing threat and the FATF standards, sources of terrorist funds, movement and storage of funds, risk-based protection of the non-profit sector, proliferation financing networks, targeted financial sanctions, financial intelligence and information sharing, and prosecution and disruption.
Intended Audience: FIU analysts and counter-terrorism financial investigators
Prosecutors, intelligence officers and sanctions implementation officials
Customs, export control and non-profit oversight officials working on terrorist or proliferation financing
Learning Objectives: Explain the terrorist and proliferation financing threat and the FATF standards that address it
Analyse how terrorist and proliferation networks raise, move and store funds
Assess non-profit sector risk proportionately, without disrupting legitimate activity
Apply targeted financial sanctions, including identifying and freezing assets
Develop financial intelligence and investigative strategies for these cases
Share intelligence and coordinate disruption with domestic and international partners
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines an expert briefing with case studies and analytical exercises, ending in a multi-agency workshop, and modules can be selected or tailored to the national threat picture.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Substantial experience of financial intelligence, counter-terrorism or financial crime investigation is helpful. Familiarity with the FATF standards is assumed.
Core Reading: FATF (2019), Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment Guidance
FATF (2023), Best Practices on Combating the Abuse of Non-Profit Organisations
FATF (2021), Guidance on Proliferation Financing Risk Assessment and Mitigation
FATF (2013), International Best Practices: Targeted Financial Sanctions Related to Terrorism and Terrorist Financing (Recommendation 6)

modules.title: The Threat and the International Framework
modules.summary: The evolving terrorist and proliferation financing threat, how it differs from money laundering, and the FATF standards and United Nations sanctions regimes that frame the national response.
objectives: Explain how terrorist and proliferation financing differ from money laundering
Summarise FATF Recommendations 5 to 8 and the related Immediate Outcomes
Assess risk assessment findings on terrorist and proliferation financing
syllabus: Small sums, legitimate sources and the purpose-based offence
FATF Recommendations 5 to 8 and Immediate Outcomes 9 to 11
United Nations Security Council targeted sanctions regimes
Terrorist and proliferation financing risk assessment

modules.title: Sources of Terrorist Funds
modules.summary: How terrorist organisations, small cells and lone actors raise funds, from legitimate income and abuse of donations to criminal activity, extortion and state sponsorship.
objectives: Identify the principal sources of terrorist funding
Distinguish the financing needs of organisations, cells and individuals
Recognise the links between terrorist financing and organised crime
syllabus: Legitimate income, self-funding and personal credit
Criminal activity, extortion and control of territory
Donations, crowdfunding and abuse of social media
State sponsorship and the crime–terror nexus

modules.title: Movement and Storage of Funds
modules.summary: The channels used to move and store terrorist funds, including banks, money service businesses, informal value transfer, cash couriers and crypto-assets, and the financial indicators they may leave.
objectives: Describe the channels used to move and store terrorist funds
Identify relevant indicators in financial and payment data
Assess the use of new payment methods and crypto-assets
syllabus: Banks, money service businesses and informal value transfer
Cash couriers and cross-border cash movements
Prepaid cards, online payments and crypto-assets
Financial indicators and their limitations

modules.title: The Non-Profit Sector: Risk-Based Protection
modules.summary: How non-profit organisations can be abused for terrorist financing, how to identify the subset at risk, and how to act proportionately without disrupting legitimate humanitarian and charitable work.
objectives: Explain FATF Recommendation 8 and the risk-based approach to non-profits
Identify the forms of abuse and the organisations most at risk
Avoid unintended consequences, including de-risking and financial exclusion
syllabus: Forms of abuse: diversion, affiliation, false representation and sham organisations
Identifying the subset of non-profits at risk
Outreach, oversight and investigation of abuse
Unintended consequences and humanitarian safeguards

modules.title: Proliferation Financing Networks
modules.summary: How networks finance the procurement of weapons of mass destruction and dual-use goods, conceal their activity through front companies and shipping, and how investigators identify them.
objectives: Explain how proliferation networks procure goods and move funds
Recognise indicators of proliferation financing and sanctions evasion
Link financial, trade and export control information
syllabus: Procurement networks, dual-use goods and front companies
Sanctions evasion through trade, shipping and corporate structures
Proliferation financing risk indicators
Working with export control and customs authorities

modules.title: Targeted Financial Sanctions in Practice
modules.summary: How targeted financial sanctions work from designation to freezing and delisting, how authorities identify and freeze assets without delay, and how breaches are investigated.
objectives: Explain designation, freezing obligations and exemptions
Identify assets of designated persons, including those held indirectly
Investigate and respond to sanctions breaches and circumvention
syllabus: Designation, proposal and listing processes
Freezing without delay and ownership and control tests
Licences, exemptions and delisting
Investigating breaches and circumvention

modules.title: Financial Intelligence and Information Sharing
modules.summary: How financial intelligence supports counter-terrorism and counter-proliferation work, from urgent reporting and rapid analysis to sharing with intelligence services, foreign FIUs and the private sector.
objectives: Apply financial intelligence techniques to terrorist and proliferation cases
Manage urgent requests and time-critical financial information
Share intelligence securely across agencies, borders and with the private sector
syllabus: Financial profiling of subjects and networks
Urgent reporting, rapid analysis and monitoring
Sharing with intelligence services, foreign FIUs and through the Egmont Group
Public-private partnerships on terrorist and proliferation financing

modules.title: Prosecution, Disruption and Multi-Agency Workshop
modules.summary: Brings the programme together by examining prosecution and disruption options, ending with a workshop in which teams develop a coordinated response to a terrorist or proliferation financing case.
objectives: Compare prosecution, sanctions and administrative disruption options
Build the evidence needed for terrorist financing charges
Agree a coordinated multi-agency response to a realistic case
syllabus: Terrorist financing offences and evidential challenges
Using intelligence as evidence and protecting sources
Disruption: freezing, designation and administrative measures
Workshop: a coordinated multi-agency response

related.title: Asset Recovery: Tracing, Freezing and Confiscation
related.summary: An eight-module programme equipping practitioners to trace, restrain, confiscate, manage and return criminal assets, including crypto-assets and assets held abroad.

related.title: Financial Investigation: Following the Money
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping investigators and analysts to run parallel financial investigations, trace funds through accounts and corporate vehicles, and present financial evidence.

related.title: FIU Operational and Strategic Analysis
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping FIU analysts to prioritise and analyse reports, produce operational and strategic intelligence, and cooperate effectively at home and abroad.

related.title: Fraud and Cyber-Enabled Financial Crime Investigations
related.summary: An eight-module programme equipping investigators and FIU analysts to tackle fraud, money mules and ransomware proceeds, working with banks and payment firms to recover funds.

related.title: Prosecuting Financial Crime: Evidence, Experts and the Courtroom
related.summary: An eight-module programme equipping prosecutors and judges to handle money laundering and complex financial crime cases, from charge and evidence to sentencing and confiscation.

related.title: Public-Private Partnerships and Financial Intelligence Sharing
related.summary: A six-module programme equipping FIUs and law-enforcement agencies to design, run and evaluate public-private partnerships for sharing financial intelligence lawfully and effectively.
